input:
For a binary distillation separating ethanol from water, the Fenske equation yields a minimum stage count of 11.7 theoretical stages, the reboiler included. The calculation proceeds on a relative volatility of 1.95, taken as constant throughout the column. The specifications are a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and bottoms containing 2 mol% of the light component.

The Fenske equation relates the number of stages to the separation accomplished at the two ends of the column, set against the relative volatility: a sharper specification at either end increases the count, and a volatility lying closer to unity increases it quite steeply. The count which the equation delivers is, moreover, the number of stages at total reflux, under which no product is withdrawn and the separation accomplished at each stage attains its maximum. The figure is consequently a minimum in the strict sense: no column separating the stated mixture to the stated specifications can operate with fewer stages, whatever reflux it is given, and every column in practice operates with more. The calculation rests, in addition, on the treatment of the relative volatility as a single number, whereas over an actual column the volatility varies with composition and temperature, and the constant value of 1.95 is the figure with which the calculation is charged for the column as a whole.

The design as proposed does not operate at total reflux. It instead employs a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux is obtained from a separate simulation of the column. The Fenske count of 11.7 stages thus bounds the design from below: the simulated count must exceed it, and a simulated count at or below the minimum would betray an error in one of the two calculations. The minimum is reported with the specifications to which it pertains, since the count varies with the specifications and has no meaning apart from them.
